## 1.5 RNA, microRNA and AGO2

- A gene's DNA is copied into a messenger RNA (**mRNA**), which the cell uses to make a protein. RNA is written in A, C, G and U; U takes the place of DNA's T
- **AGO2** is a protein that holds a **microRNA**, an RNA of about 22 letters. It binds mRNAs that pair with that microRNA (A with U, G with C), and the bound mRNA yields less protein
- Our sequences are RNA, so the notebooks use U; the DNA models of part 2 read T

::: {.notes}
- Projected: 2 min (a recap if the opening lecture covered it).
- Where AGO2 binds, the mRNA is degraded or not translated.
- Humans have several hundred microRNAs; each can regulate hundreds of genes.
:::

## 1.6 The seed rule

- AGO2 carries a microRNA. Its **seed** (letters 2 to 7) pairs with the target mRNA; this site also pairs letter 8

![](assets/custom/seed_pairing.png){fig-align="center" height="432px"}

::: {.notes}
- Projected: 1 min.
- The top row is a real bound sequence from our data. It contains the miR-16 site UGCUGCU, which pairs with microRNA letters 2 to 8.
- Hypothesis for the day: a model that learned AGO2 targeting should respond to seed sites like this one. The last slide of this part tests it (an optional cell in the notebook).
:::

## 1.7 The data

- **Bound**: about 48,000 sites where CLIP-seq found AGO2 (AGO2 is crosslinked to the RNA it touches, pulled down, and that RNA is sequenced). **Unbound**: about 44,000 random positions in the same genes
- Each sequence is about 330 letters, with the 40-letter measured site at letters 150 to 190

![](assets/custom/labels_raster.png){fig-align="center" height="492px"}

::: {.notes}
- Projected: 2 min.
- CLIP-seq: UV light crosslinks proteins to the RNA they touch, an antibody pulls down AGO2, and the attached RNA fragments are sequenced.
- The data set is the GraphProt CLIP benchmark (Maticzka et al. 2014), used by Pan and Shen (2018), whose CNN we follow. The unbound sequences are the bound sites moved to random positions in the same genes.
- 99% of sequences have the measured site starting exactly at letter 150. Sequences are 137 to 375 letters long.
- Each row is one sequence, dark for G or C, light for A or U; 150 of each class, sorted by G+C. The white stripes on the right are sequence ends.
- The bound half is slightly richer in A and U: mean G+C 0.41 vs 0.45 over all sequences. AGO2 sites are often in AU-rich 3′ UTRs (the part of an mRNA after its protein-coding letters), so part of this may be biology and part may come from how the unbound positions were drawn. Part 3 tests that.
:::

## 1.8 Seed matches are enriched in bound sites

![](assets/custom/kmer_enrichment.png){fig-align="center" height="700px"}

::: {.notes}
- Projected: 2 min.
- Counted inside the 40-letter measured sites: for every 7-letter word, the fraction of bound sites that contain it divided by the fraction of unbound sites. The 16 most enriched words.
- The top word, UUUGCAC, is the seed match of miR-19 (6 times enriched). miR-30 (UGUUUAC) and miR-15/16 (UGCUGCU, and GCUGCUA, which pairs letters 2 to 7) are also in the list.
- Even the most enriched word occurs in only 1 to 2% of bound sites, so no single word separates the classes.
- A model that learned AGO2 targeting should respond to these words. This part ends by testing whether our CNN does.
:::

::: {.center}
# 2 Learning and testing {data-name="Learning"}
:::

## 2.1 What training does

- Model: $\;\hat p = \sigma(w^\top x + b)$, with $x$ = (G+C fraction, U fraction)
- Training: compute the gradient of the loss, move $w, b$ against it, repeat
- $\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$ turns any score into a probability between 0 and 1. **Loss**: binary cross-entropy, minus the log of the probability given to the true label

![](assets/custom/lr_training.png){fig-align="center" height="480px"}

::: {.notes}
- The smallest possible model on our data: two features per sequence and three parameters. The line is where the predicted probability equals 0.5.
- Our CNN has 2,491 parameters. The genome models have millions to billions.
- The loss is binary cross-entropy; a coin flip gives 0.69. Here it falls from 0.77 at a deliberately bad start to 0.67. Slide 2.4 measures how much (0.66).
- Every model today ends with a sigmoid.
:::

## 2.2 Train, validate, test

- **Train**: fit the parameters
- **Validation**: choose settings, such as the number of epochs (passes over the training data)
- **Test**: report once; never used for choices
- Parts 1 and 2 use the same **1,000 held-out sequences** (500 bound, 500 unbound) as the test set

::: {.notes}
- Never grade a model on the data it was trained on.
- The notebook prints the held-out AUROC after every epoch, so we do look at the test set during training. That is acceptable for a workshop as long as nobody picks the best epoch by it; in a real project that is the validation set's job.
- The split is random by sequence. We checked for near-duplicates: 47% of held-out bound sequences have a training sequence within 150 letters on the genome (13% of unbound). On the 698 held-out sequences without one, the CNN scores 0.85 instead of 0.86, so the effect on our results is small. Real projects split by gene or chromosome.
:::

## 2.3 AUROC

- **AUROC** = the probability that a random bound sequence scores higher than a random unbound one. 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.

![](assets/custom/auroc.png){fig-align="center" height="596px"}

::: {.notes}
- These are the scores of the CNN we build in the next section; for now it is any model that outputs a probability.
- Left: the CNN's scores on the 1,000 held-out sequences, bound in blue and unbound in grey.
- Each threshold on the left gives one true positive rate and one false positive rate, one point on the right. The area under the curve is the AUROC.
- It does not depend on a threshold, so it compares models fairly. It says nothing about why a model scores well.
- For anyone who knows diagnostic tests: this is the ROC curve, sensitivity against 1 minus specificity.
:::

## 2.4 Noise in a held-out AUROC

- On 1,000 test sequences, 95% of resampled AUROCs fall within about **±0.025**

![](assets/custom/auroc_ci.png){fig-align="center" height="642px"}

::: {.notes}
- Resample the 1,000 test sequences with replacement 2,000 times; the bar covers 95% of the resulting AUROCs.
- Three models from today: the CNN (0.86), logistic regression on 5-letter word counts (0.74), and on the two composition numbers of slide 2.1 (0.66). The bars do not overlap, so these differences are larger than the sampling noise.
- The bars describe one model at a time. Two models scored on the same sequences make correlated errors, so their difference varies less than the bars suggest; a paired bootstrap measures it. Overlapping bars mean no evidence of a difference, not proof that the models are equal.
- Rule of thumb: on 1,000 test sequences ignore differences below about 0.03; on 3,000 (part 3), below about 0.02.
:::

## 2.5 Overfitting

- A model that scores much higher on its training data than on held-out data has **overfit**: it memorised its training examples. Report the held-out score

![](assets/custom/probe_trap.png){fig-align="center" height="596px"}

::: {.notes}
- The same model, logistic regression on 5-letter word counts, scored two ways.
- Left: 12,000 training sequences with regularisation. 0.82 on its own training data, 0.74 held out. A small gap is normal.
- Right: 600 sequences and almost no regularisation. 1.00 on its training data, 0.67 held out.
- Regularisation penalises large weights, which limits how closely a model can fit its training data.
- In any evaluation code, including code an AI assistant wrote, check first which data the score was computed on.

Next: build the CNN.
:::

::: {.center}
# 3 The CNN {data-name="CNN"}
:::

## 3.1 One-hot encoding (TODO-1)

- Each letter becomes a column with a single 1 in its row (A, C, G, U): a sequence becomes a $4 \times \text{length}$ matrix
- All sequences are padded to 501 columns with columns of 0.25 (the longest is 375 letters)

![](assets/custom/onehot_big.png){fig-align="center" height="492px"}

::: {.notes}
- TODO-1 encodes one sequence and checks its first columns against its letters.
- If asked why not A=1, C=2, G=3, U=4: that would impose an order (G "greater than" C) with no biological meaning. One-hot keeps the four letters equally far apart.
- A padding column of 0.25 means "unknown letter": each base equally likely. 501 is the input width used by Pan and Shen, whose CNN this one follows.
:::

## 3.2 A filter computes a dot product

![](assets/custom/filter_dot.png){fig-align="center" height="700px"}

::: {.notes}
- A real learned filter (filter 7) from the trained CNN, applied to the real window where it responds most strongly.
- The filter is a 4 × 10 matrix of weights, one per letter and position. Multiplied element by element with the one-hot window, it keeps one weight per position: the weight of the letter that is there. Their sum plus a bias is the filter's output at that position.
- The same 40 weights are applied at every one of the 492 positions. Sharing the weights across positions is what makes it a convolution.
- This filter prefers U-rich windows, and its strongest response is only 1.07 times larger on bound than on unbound sequences. It responds to something common in both classes. Part 3 tests composition effects of this kind with a shuffle and with matched data.
:::

## 3.3 The filter along one sequence

- **ReLU**: $\max(0, z)$, so negative outputs become 0

![](assets/custom/activation_track.png){fig-align="center" height="642px"}

::: {.notes}
- The same filter's output at every position of one bound sequence, after ReLU.
- Most positions give 0. Windows that resemble the weights give large values. The highest one is marked and its letters printed.
:::

## 3.4 The network (TODO-2)

| Layer | Output shape |
|:--|:--|
| input | $1 \times 4 \times 501$ |
| `Conv2d(1, 10, (4, 10))` + ReLU | $10 \times 1 \times 492$ |
| `MaxPool2d((1, 3))` | $10 \times 1 \times 164$ |
| `Conv2d(10, 20, (1, 5))` + ReLU | $20 \times 1 \times 160$ |
| `MaxPool2d((1, 3))` | $20 \times 1 \times 53$ |
| `Flatten` → `Linear(1060, 1)` | one score, a **logit** (any real number) |

- 2,491 parameters. No sigmoid inside the network: `BCEWithLogitsLoss` applies it.

::: {.notes}
- 10 first-layer filters, each 4 × 10. Each produces one output row, a channel.
- Max pooling keeps the largest value in each block of 3 positions.
- The second convolution combines nearby first-layer outputs: 20 channels, each looking at 5 pooled positions.
- The final linear layer has one weight per channel and pooled position: 20 × 53 = 1,060 weights. Slide 5.2 shows them after training.
- A logit is any real number; the sigmoid turns it into a probability between 0 and 1.
:::

## 3.5 Training changes the filters

$$\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \, \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}$$

![](assets/custom/filter_learning.png){fig-align="center" height="605px"}

::: {.notes}
- One filter at epochs 0, 1, 3 and 10 of a training run, with the held-out AUROC after each epoch.
- Epoch 0 is the random initialisation (AUROC 0.58). By epoch 10 the filter has a clear preference and the model reaches 0.86.
- Each step computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight and moves each weight against its gradient, scaled by the learning rate $\eta$. We use Adam, a variant that adapts the step size per weight.
:::

## 3.6 The training step and the evaluation (TODO-3)

```python
opt.zero_grad()                       # clear the previous step's gradients
loss = criterion(model(X), y)         # predict a batch, measure the error
loss.backward()                       # gradient of the loss for every weight
opt.step()                            # move every weight against its gradient

model.eval()                          # evaluation mode
with torch.no_grad():                 # no gradients, no learning
    probs = torch.sigmoid(model(X_test.to(DEVICE))).cpu().numpy()
auc = roc_auc_score(test_y, probs)
```

::: {.notes}
- The first four lines are given in the notebook. TODO-3 is the evaluation block.
- `.cpu().numpy()` matters: scikit-learn cannot read a tensor that is still on the GPU, a common error in this TODO.
:::

::: {.center}
# 4 Look inside {data-name="Look inside"}
:::

## 4.1 From a filter to a sequence logo (TODO-4)

- `cutoff_for` → `windows_above` → `pwm_of` → logo: collect the windows with the highest output, count letters per position
- Logo height = information content: 2 bits = always the same letter, 0 = all four equally often

![](assets/custom/filter_logo.png){fig-align="center" height="492px"}

::: {.notes}
- Left: filter 0's 40 weights. Right: its logo, built from the roughly 25,000 windows in bound sequences whose output is above the cutoff (half-way between the filter's mean and maximum output). The notebook's count differs slightly because it scans a different subset.
- Information content at a position is 2 minus the entropy of the letter frequencies, in bits. Each letter's height is its frequency times that value.
- A logo shows which windows activate a filter. It leaves out the letters the filter penalises (its negative weights).
- TODO-4 builds a logo for every filter with these helpers, then `consensus_of` reads off the most frequent letter at each position.
:::

## 4.2 Test a logo: insert it, against a shuffled copy (TODO-5)

- Take the consensus of one filter (its most frequent letter at each position), a candidate **motif**, and insert it 1 to 7 times into 1,000 random RNA sequences, and score them
- **Control**: the same letters in shuffled order, inserted at the same places
- Compare the two curves; the shuffled copy has the same letters, so the difference is what the order adds

::: {.notes}
- Projected: 1 min.
- `plant(seqs, motif, copies)` writes copy n starting at letter 40 + 45(n − 1); 7 copies fit in a 330-letter sequence.
- This turns a logo, which is only a description of what a filter responds to, into an experiment on the whole model's output.
:::

## 5.2 The last layer weighs positions

![](assets/custom/last_layer.png){fig-align="center" height="700px"}

::: {.notes}
- The trained last-layer weights: one row per channel, one column per pooled position. Our run; the notebook does not draw this.
- Pooled column j covers letters of roughly 9j to 9j + 29. The large weights sit in columns 17 to 20, letters about 150 to 210: where the measured site sits in almost every sequence.
- The columns on the right are padding (no sequence is longer than 375 letters), so their weights barely move from initialisation.
- The CNN learned where in the sequence to look, as well as which letter patterns to look for. Slide 5.6 shows what that implies.

## 5.5 Insert the motif

![](assets/custom/dose_response.png){fig-align="center" height="700px"}

::: {.notes}
- 1,000 random RNA sequences. The dotted line is their mean score with nothing inserted.
- Insert the motif 1 to 7 times (black), the most that fit in a 330-letter sequence, and the same letters in shuffled order (grey). Compare the two curves rather than each curve with the baseline: the shuffled copy has the same letters, so it also changes the score.
- `plant()` writes copy n starting at letter 40 + 45(n − 1). The score jumps when copy 4 (letter 175) lands in the region the CNN weighs and decreases slightly with more copies (0.72 to 0.68), as they replace more of the background.
:::

## 5.6 Position matters

![](assets/custom/position_scan.png){fig-align="center" height="700px"}

::: {.notes}
- One copy of the motif at every position, averaged over 400 random sequences (a given cell in the notebook). The numbers 1 to 7 mark where `plant()` puts each copy in the previous test.
- The motif changes the score only between about letters 140 and 190, where almost every sequence in the data has its measured site (shaded).
- The shuffled copy gets much of the same increase there, so a good part of the effect comes from which letters sit in that region, whatever their order.
- This is the last-layer pattern from slide 5.2: the CNN weighs positions. It reflects how the data were cut, and it means the answer to "does this motif matter?" depends on where it is placed.
:::

## 5.7 The CNN responds to one of four seed sites

![](assets/custom/planting_bars.png){fig-align="center" height="700px"}

::: {.notes}
- The hypothesis from slide 1.6: a model that learned AGO2 targeting should respond to seed sites. This is the optional bonus cell.
- 6 copies of each site inserted into real unbound sequences, against the same letters shuffled (grey: mean and standard deviation over 10 shuffles).
- miR-15/16 (UGCUGCU): 0.53 against 0.31 ± 0.09, a clear effect. miR-19, miR-30 and let-7 lie within the spread of their shuffles.
- The CNN was not given seed sites and responds to one of the four tested. None of the ten logos shows this site; the insertion test detected the response.
- Inside the 40-letter measured site, these seed sites are 3 to 6 times enriched in bound sequences but occur in only about 1 to 2% of them, so the signal is weak.
- The notebook's shuffle numbers differ slightly from these because the shuffles are random.
